scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated during the Edo period, influenced by the dances of visiting sailors.
By the middle of the eighteenth century, it had become a performance showcase for local girls.

In 1976, the Japanese government designated it as an intangible cultural heritage, and in 2009, it was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, later being incorporated into the Furyu-odori category in 2022.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is performed to celebrate the New Year and to invoke good fortune, specifically targeting prosperity and abundant fishing catches for the community.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Ten to twenty girls, aged 5 to 12, perform in two rows facing each other or in a circle.
They hold bamboo strips in their hands and strike them together to create a rhythmic sound.
The dancers are accompanied by an a cappella choir of older women.
Watch for Bamboo clicking.

Captions name each signature move as it appears

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is provided entirely by an a cappella choir of five to ten older women.
The only instrumental element is the rhythmic clicking of bamboo strips held by the dancers, which produces the signature sound of the performance.
Listen for the Bamboo strips.
The music is defined by the contrast between the melodic a cappella singing of older women and the sharp, percussive clicking of bamboo strips held by the young dancers.
